She had forgotten one of the steps

pages.text: Every evening after dinner, Faris heard his grandfather humming the same gentle tune on the balcony. It was a melody that seemed to belong to another time, slow and full of longing. One hot afternoon, while helping his mother clear out the storeroom, Faris noticed a long black case hidden behind some old carpets. When he opened it, a cloud of dust rose into the air. Inside lay an oud with a deep crack running across its face, and every one of its strings was missing.

Faris carried the case to the balcony, expecting his grandfather to be delighted. Instead, the old man's face fell, and for a long moment he said nothing. "That was my father's gift to me," he finally explained. "It was damaged when we moved house forty years ago, and I haven't played since." Faris asked whether it could be repaired, but his grandfather simply shook his head. "Some things can't be fixed, habibi," he said quietly. "Put it back where you found it."

Faris couldn't get the broken instrument out of his mind. After searching online for hours, he discovered that an elderly craftsman named Uncle Saleh still had a tiny workshop in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. The next Friday, his older cousin drove him through the narrow streets until they found a wooden door decorated with carved patterns. Uncle Saleh examined the oud carefully, turning it over in his rough hands. "I can help you," he said at last, "but I won't do the work for you. If you want it done, you'll have to be patient and get your own hands dirty."

For the next six weeks, Faris spent every weekend in the dusty workshop. He learned how to remove old glue, how to sand wood without damaging it, and how to fill a crack so thinly that it could hardly be seen. More than once he felt he had bitten off more than he could chew, especially when a whole afternoon's work had to be done again. "Slow down," Uncle Saleh told him whenever he rushed. "Wood remembers every mistake you make, but it also remembers every bit of care." Gradually, Faris began to understand that patience was a skill, just like any other.

One afternoon, while Faris was cleaning the inside of the instrument with a small light, he noticed some faded pencil marks. He held his breath as he read the words, written in careful Arabic script. "For my son Abdullah, so that his hands are never silent." Underneath was a date from more than sixty years earlier. Abdullah was his grandfather's name. Uncle Saleh leaned over to look and smiled. "Your great-grandfather has been waiting a long time for someone to read that message," he said.

Faris now had a new goal: he wanted to play his grandfather's tune when he returned the oud. The problem was that he had never touched an instrument in his life. With his mother's help, he recorded his grandfather humming on the balcony, pretending he was only filming the sunset. Uncle Saleh, who turned out to be a skilled player, taught him how to hold the risha and find the notes. Faris practised until his fingertips were sore, playing the melody again and again until it no longer sounded completely out of tune.

Two days before his grandfather's birthday, disaster struck. As Faris was tightening the final string, the small wooden bridge suddenly snapped with a sharp crack. His heart sank, and he was sure that all his hard work had been for nothing. However, Uncle Saleh didn't panic at all. "If I'd given up every time something broke, I'd have closed this shop fifty years ago," he laughed, reaching for a fresh piece of wood. They worked together late into the evening, and by the time the call to prayer echoed across the old city, the oud was complete.

On the evening of the birthday, the whole family gathered in the living room. Faris placed the black case in front of his grandfather, who looked puzzled until he lifted the lid. The old man ran his fingers over the smooth, repaired face, and his eyes filled with tears. When Faris showed him the hidden message, he had to sit down. Then, with trembling hands, Faris began to play the familiar tune. He made several mistakes, but nobody in the room seemed to notice.

When the last note faded, his grandfather slowly held out his hands for the oud. At first his fingers were stiff and unsure, as though they had forgotten everything. Then, little by little, the melody came back to him, richer and more beautiful than Faris had ever imagined. After a while, he passed the instrument back to his grandson and began to hum along as Faris played. "You were wrong, Grandpa," Faris said with a grin. "Some things can be fixed." His grandfather smiled and replied, "Yes, but only by someone who refuses to give up."

options: Behind some old carpets in the storeroom

options: He wanted Faris to learn patience and do the work himself
He was too old and tired to work
He thought the oud could not be fixed

What was written inside the oud?
options: The name of the shop where it was made
A message from Faris's great-grandfather to his son
The notes of Grandpa's favourite tune

options: He was angry that Faris had taken the oud
He felt that his broken past had been healed and he was happy to play again

pages.text: Every summer, Faris spent his mornings helping his grandfather in a tiny oud shop in Al-Balad, the old heart of Jeddah. The shop smelled of sandalwood, roses and centuries of history, and Faris had grown to love every corner of it. Its greatest treasure was a dark, heavy block of rare agarwood that had been kept in a glass case for over twenty years. Grandfather liked to say it was worth more than a new car. "Some things," he would add with a smile, "are worth more than money, too."

On Thursday morning, Faris unlocked the door and froze: the glass case was empty. Strangely, the lock had not been broken, and nothing else in the shop had been touched. When Grandfather arrived, his face turned pale and he had to sit down. Only three people had been inside the shop the evening before. There was Hamza, the young assistant who had his own key, Mr Saleem, a wealthy customer who had asked to hold the agarwood, and Nabil, the delivery man who had brought boxes of rosewater bottles.

Grandfather didn't want to call the police until he was sure, because he couldn't bear to accuse an innocent person. "Give me until the evening prayer," Faris begged, and his cousin Yousef immediately offered to help. The boys searched the shop slowly, and Faris noticed something odd near the pile of empty rosewater crates by the back door. Even though the crates should have smelled of roses, the air around them was heavy with the deep, smoky scent of oud. It was much stronger there than anywhere else in the room. "Either I'm imagining things," Faris whispered, "or something has been hidden here."

First, they spoke to Hamza, who looked so nervous that Yousef was sure he was guilty. After a long silence, Hamza admitted that he had stepped out to buy tea the evening before, leaving the shop unattended for about ten minutes. He had been too embarrassed to tell anyone, especially now that the agarwood was missing. "I know I should have stayed," he said, staring at the floor. Faris believed him, but he wrote down one important detail: the spare key to the glass case always hung on a hook behind the counter.

Next, Grandfather phoned Mr Saleem, who explained calmly that he had held the agarwood for a minute and then handed it back. Grandfather remembered locking the case himself afterwards, so Mr Saleem seemed to be telling the truth. Then Faris asked a question that changed everything. "When is Nabil coming back?" Grandfather checked his notebook and frowned. "This afternoon, to collect the empty crates," he replied slowly.

Faris lifted the crates one by one, and the third felt surprisingly heavy for something that was supposed to be empty. Underneath a layer of straw, wrapped in an old cloth, lay the precious agarwood. Suddenly the whole picture made sense to him. While Hamza was out buying tea, Nabil must have taken the spare key, opened the case, and hidden the wood inside a crate he planned to take away the next day. Nobody would ever search a box of empty bottles, or so he had thought.

Yousef wanted to confront Nabil the moment he walked in, but Faris had a better idea. They replaced the agarwood with an ordinary piece of wood of the same size and weight, and covered it with straw again. Meanwhile, Grandfather quietly called an old friend who worked as a police officer and asked him to wait outside. When Nabil arrived that afternoon, he chatted about the heat as if nothing had happened. However, he picked up the third crate first and walked towards his van a little too quickly.

The officer stopped him in the narrow street and asked to see inside the crate. Nabil laughed nervously, but when the straw was pulled away, his smile disappeared. "That's not the right wood!" he shouted, before he could stop himself. There was a long, uncomfortable silence as he realised what he had just said. In the end, he confessed that he had owed money to some people and had hoped to sell the agarwood in another city.

That evening, the agarwood was back in its case, and Grandfather made everyone sweet mint tea. He told Hamza that honesty mattered more than any mistake, and Hamza promised he would never leave the shop alone again. Then Grandfather placed a small, fragrant piece of oud in Faris's hand. "Most detectives trust only their eyes," he said, "but you followed your nose, and it led you straight to the truth." Faris grinned, already wondering what mystery next summer might bring.

questions.q: Why didn't Grandfather call the police immediately?
options: He didn't want to accuse an innocent person.
He thought the agarwood was not valuable.
The police station was closed on Thursday.

options: They smelled strongly of oud instead of roses.

options: They showed he was angry with the officer.

pages.text: The first time it happened, Faris was reaching for a glass of mango juice that his little brother had knocked off the kitchen table. He held his breath, squeezed his fist, and suddenly the glass simply stopped in the air, like a photograph. The clock on the wall had frozen, his mother's voice had disappeared halfway through a word, and even the steam above the teapot hung perfectly still. Faris counted in his head, his heart racing, and on the count of ten everything crashed back into motion. By then he had already caught the glass, and nobody had the faintest idea how he had done it.

Over the following weeks, Faris tested his strange gift again and again until he understood the rules. He could stop the world for exactly ten seconds, no more and no less, and then he had to wait an hour before he could do it again. He had been tempted, more than once, to use it in a maths test, but each time he decided that a win he hadn't earned wasn't worth having. Instead, he filled a whole notebook with drawings of a superhero called The Pause, who wore a silver mask and saved entire cities. In his imagination, the whole country was talking about The Pause.

One Friday evening, the family drove up to Grandma Noura's house in Taif, where the air smelled of roses and fresh bread. After dinner, there was exactly one piece of kunafa left on the plate, and Faris and his cousin Saud both had their eyes on it. With a small, guilty smile, Faris held his breath and froze the room. He was just lifting the plate when a calm voice behind him said, "That isn't very polite, habibi." Faris spun around, his mouth hanging open, because Grandma Noura was the only other person in the room who was still moving.

Later, when everyone else had gone to bed, his grandmother poured two cups of tea and told him everything. She had discovered the same gift when she was thirteen, and she had used it many times throughout her life, although never in front of anyone. "Every young person with this gift makes the same mistake," she said gently. "They think ten seconds is time to run, to fight, to show off." She tapped the side of her head and smiled. "Ten seconds isn't for running, Faris. It's for thinking."

The following morning, the whole family went to the busy market in the old part of the city to buy rose water and honey. The street there sloped steeply downhill, and it was packed with shoppers, children and stalls piled high with fruit. Suddenly, Faris heard a horrible scraping sound and turned to see a delivery truck rolling down the hill with no driver inside. It was picking up speed, and right in its path, a small boy was crouching on the road, completely focused on a ball he had dropped. People began to scream, but in the blink of an eye, Faris had already held his breath.

The world went silent and grey, and Faris ran straight at the truck and pushed against it with all his strength. Nothing happened, of course; it weighed several tonnes, and he was a fourteen-year-old boy in trainers. Panic rose in his chest as he realised that five whole seconds had already been wasted. Then his grandmother's words came back to him: it's for thinking. He looked at the truck properly for the first time and noticed that the driver's window had been left wide open.

Faris reached through the window, grabbed the handbrake and pulled it up as hard as he possibly could. Seven seconds. He sprinted to the little boy, lifted him carefully onto the pavement, and placed the ball in his hands. Nine seconds. He had only just stepped back into his original place in the crowd when the sound and colour of the world came rushing back. The truck jerked violently, its wheels screeched, and it came to a stop barely a metre from where the boy had been sitting.

For a moment, nobody moved, and then everybody started talking at once. The boy's father hugged his son tightly, thanking God again and again, while the driver ran up the hill, pale and out of breath. "I'm sure I pulled the brake," he kept saying, scratching his head in confusion. One man insisted the boy must have jumped out of the way by himself, and an old shopkeeper declared it was a miracle. Not a single person looked at Faris, and he felt a strange mixture of pride and disappointment, because nobody would ever know the truth.

Then he felt a familiar hand on his shoulder, and he looked up to see Grandma Noura smiling at him. "Seven seconds," she whispered. "That's much faster than I was at your age." That night, Faris opened his notebook, looked at his drawings of The Pause for a long time, and then turned to a clean page. He didn't draw a mask or a cape; instead, he wrote just one line in careful handwriting: Don't run. Think. Some heroes are seen by the whole world, he decided, but the best ones only need ten quiet seconds and a clear head.

Why didn't Faris use his gift during his maths test?

options: He had saved the boy, but nobody knew he was the hero

stories.title: The Thief of the Red Dunes

pages.text: By the time the family's two cars had climbed the last red dune, the sun was already sinking behind the Nafud desert. Fourteen-year-old Layla jumped out first, breathing in the cool, clean air that smelled of sand and distant rain. Her younger brother Omar, on the other hand, was frowning at his phone and holding it up as if the sky might offer him a signal. "No network," he groaned. "Three whole days with no network." Grandmother Huda, who had been camping in this desert since she was a girl, simply laughed and handed him a tent pole.

Setting up camp took longer than anyone had expected, mainly because Uncle Saad insisted on reading the instructions aloud. Eventually, though, the tents were standing, the rugs were spread out and a kettle of cardamom coffee was bubbling over the fire. Layla lay back on a rug and stared at the sky, which was gradually filling with more stars than she had ever seen in Riyadh. Before going to sleep, Omar carefully placed his phone, his charger and his power bank in a neat row beside his sleeping bag. "Nobody touches these," he warned, looking directly at his sister.

The next morning, Layla was woken by a furious shout: "My charger's gone!" Omar was standing outside the tent, his hair sticking up in every direction. It turned out that he wasn't the only victim, because Uncle Saad's favourite sock had vanished and a silver spoon was missing from the cooking box. Omar narrowed his eyes at Layla. "You've been teasing me about my phone all week, so just admit it." "Don't jump to conclusions," she replied coolly, although she couldn't help smiling.

Grandmother Huda didn't join the argument. Instead, she crouched down near the tents and studied the sand, which was covered in tiny marks that nobody else had noticed. "Whoever took your things," she said quietly, "has four legs and very small feet." She pointed to a line of neat prints, each no bigger than a coin, leading away towards the dunes. "When I was your age, my father taught me to read the sand the way you read your messages," she added, winking at Omar.

That afternoon, while the adults rested in the shade, the two of them followed the tracks. At first it felt like looking for a needle in a haystack, because the wind kept blurring the prints. However, Layla discovered that if she looked at the sand from low down, with the sun behind it, the shadows made the footprints stand out clearly. Omar, who had stopped complaining about his phone for the first time in days, was genuinely impressed. "Okay," he admitted, "that's actually quite clever." By sunset the trail had disappeared near a rocky ridge, and they had to walk back to camp empty-handed.

Fortunately, Grandmother had a plan. "Thieves return to places where they've been successful," she explained, so that night they left a few dates and a shiny bottle cap on a rug beside the fire. Layla and Omar hid behind the car, wrapped in blankets and trying hard not to giggle or yawn. An hour passed, then another, and the fire slowly burned down to glowing orange coals. Just as Omar was about to give up, a small shape appeared at the edge of the light.

It was a fox, as pale as the sand, with enormous ears and a bushy tail tipped with white. It moved silently towards the rug, sniffed the dates and, ignoring them completely, picked up the bottle cap in its mouth. "Caught red-handed," whispered Layla. The fox froze and stared at them with shining eyes for a moment before trotting away into the darkness. This time, with the moon lighting up the sand, they were able to follow it at a safe distance.

The trail led them back to the rocky ridge, where the fox slipped into a hole beneath a large stone. Holding their breath, they crept closer and shone a torch inside, careful not to frighten it. Just inside the entrance lay an astonishing collection: a spoon, a sock, some foil wrappers, a key ring and, glowing faintly white, Omar's charger. Two fluffy cubs were curled up asleep on the sock as if it were a blanket. Omar reached for his charger, then stopped, because the cable had been chewed into three pieces.

The next morning, Grandmother came with them and carefully removed the foil and the broken cable, explaining that plastic could seriously hurt the cubs, but they left the sock exactly where it was. Uncle Saad declared that the fox could keep it, as long as it never stole the other one. That evening, Omar's phone finally died, and to everyone's surprise, he simply put it away in his bag. Then he lay back on the rug beside Layla and gazed up at the sky. "Grandmother," he said, "could you teach me to read the stars as well?" Smiling, she sat down beside them and began to point.

questions.q: Why was Omar unhappy when the family arrived at the camp?
options: He didn't want to put up the tents.
He was afraid of the dark desert.

options: Looking at the sand from low down with the sun behind it

options: seen in the middle of doing something wrong

options: Omar wanted to fix his charger.

options: He has started to enjoy the desert more than his phone.

pages.text: Faisal had always believed that he could win any argument, as long as he was on the right side of it. So when Mr. Saeed pinned the list for the inter-school debate final on the noticeboard, Faisal read it twice, convinced there had been a mistake. Not only was his usual partner, Omar, missing from the list, but Faisal had been paired with Tariq, the quiet boy who sat at the back of the library and hardly ever spoke. Worse still, they had been told to argue that schools should ban smartphones completely, an idea Faisal had criticised loudly all year. "This has to be a joke," he muttered, but deep down he knew that Mr. Saeed never joked about debates.

"Omar broke his wrist playing football," Mr. Saeed explained when Faisal found him outside the staffroom. "And Tariq has been researching this topic for months, even though nobody asked him to." Faisal opened his mouth to complain, then closed it again, because the final was only ten days away. Their opponents were Al-Noor Academy, a school that hadn't lost a debate in three years. "You don't have to agree with an argument to understand it," the teacher added, handing him a thick folder. "The best debaters never take a side until they've put themselves in the other person's shoes."

Their first meeting in the library did not go well. Faisal arrived late, dropped his bag onto the table and announced that he would do the speaking while Tariq looked after the notes. Tariq simply nodded, but when Faisal began practising his opening speech, the quiet boy interrupted him for the first time. "That statistic is out of date," he said calmly, sliding a printed article across the table. "If Al-Noor notices, they'll tear us apart." Faisal stared at the page, feeling his cheeks burn, because Tariq was absolutely right.

Over the following days, something unexpected happened. Faisal started looking forward to their sessions after the afternoon prayer, when the library was almost empty and the air conditioner hummed softly above them. Tariq, it turned out, had an excellent memory and a dry sense of humour that he only revealed once he felt comfortable. He had interviewed teachers, counted how many students checked their phones during break, and even asked his little brother to keep a diary of his screen time. "I'm not against technology," he admitted one evening. "I just think we've stopped noticing what we're missing."

That sentence stayed in Faisal's head long after he got home. That night, instead of scrolling until midnight as usual, he put his phone in a drawer and went to sit with his grandfather in the majlis. The old man told him stories about his own school days, when a single borrowed book could be passed between ten boys until its pages were soft. Faisal realised he had never asked his grandfather about any of this before. He still disagreed with a complete ban, but for the first time he understood why someone might want one.

On the day of the final, the school hall was packed with students, parents and teachers, and even the principal had taken a seat in the front row. Al-Noor's first speaker was confident and sharp, and the audience applauded loudly when she sat down. Then it was Tariq's turn to open for their team. He stood up, looked at the crowd, and froze completely, his index cards trembling in his hands. Ten seconds passed, then twenty, and Faisal could hear people beginning to whisper.

Without thinking, Faisal stood up beside his partner and asked the judges for permission to begin instead. He didn't have Tariq's notes, but he didn't need them, because he had spent ten days listening. "Two weeks ago, I would have argued against this motion," he began honestly, and the hall fell silent. He described the boys who no longer talked to each other at break, the brother who had lost hours to games, and the grandfather whose stories he had almost never heard. By the time he finished, several people in the audience were nodding.

When the time came for the final rebuttal, Faisal glanced at Tariq and gave him a small nod. Tariq took a deep breath, ignored the crowd and spoke only to the judges, as if they were sitting together in the empty library. One by one, he took apart Al-Noor's arguments with facts so precise that their captain stopped writing altogether. His voice grew stronger with every sentence, and when he sat down, the applause was even louder than before. Faisal leaned over and whispered, "I told you they'd tear somebody apart, just not us."

The judges announced that the school had won by a single point, and the hall erupted with cheers. Afterwards, the head judge told Mr. Saeed that she had never seen a team rescue each other so smoothly under pressure. On Sunday morning, when the new list went up on the noticeboard, Faisal had added a name to the top himself: Tariq, team captain. "You're sure about this?" Tariq asked, raising an eyebrow. "Completely," Faisal replied with a grin. "I've learned it's worth listening to the other side."

questions.q: Why was Faisal unhappy when he first read the list?
options: He had been paired with Tariq and given a position he disagreed with
He had not been chosen for the debate at all

questions.q: What happened to Omar?
options: He broke his wrist playing football
He decided he didn't like debating

questions.q: In the story, what does "froze" mean when Tariq stood up to speak?
options: He felt very cold in the hall
He suddenly could not move or speak

questions.q: What changed Faisal's opinion about phones?
options: Mr. Saeed ordered him to change his mind
Tariq's words and an evening talking with his grandfather
His phone broke before the final

questions.q: Why do you think Faisal made Tariq team captain?
options: Because Omar refused to come back to the team
Because he now respected Tariq's skills and had learned to listen to others
Because the principal told him to do it

stories.title: Open When the House Is Quiet

pages.text: The summer Layan turned fourteen, her family spent every weekend emptying her grandparents' old house in Al-Malaz. Since her grandmother had passed away last winter, her grandfather had hardly spoken, and the doctors had suggested he should come and live with them. Nobody argued, but everyone felt it: the house that had once been full of laughter now felt like a museum after closing time. Layan's father kept saying they had to be practical, yet he lingered over every photograph as if he couldn't bear to put it in a box.

On the last Friday, Layan and her younger brother Omar were sent to clear the storage room on the roof. Behind a pile of rolled-up carpets, Omar discovered a rusty biscuit tin, and inside it, wrapped carefully in a silk scarf, was a single cassette tape. A faded label had been stuck across it in their grandmother's elegant handwriting: 'Open when the house is quiet.' Omar raised his eyebrows dramatically and whispered, 'It's a secret message, obviously. Maybe there's treasure buried under the palm tree.' Layan rolled her eyes, but her heart had started beating faster.

The problem was that nobody owned anything that could play a cassette anymore. When they showed it to their father, he laughed and said they might as well look for a needle in a haystack. Then Omar remembered that Uncle Saad still drove his ancient Toyota, which had a tape deck he refused to replace. Unfortunately, when Uncle Saad pulled the cassette out of the tin, they saw that some of the tape had come loose and was hopelessly tangled. Patiently, Layan wound it back with a pencil, holding her breath in case it snapped.

That evening, the four of them squeezed into the car, and Uncle Saad pressed play. At first there was only a soft hiss, and then, unmistakably, their grandmother's voice filled the car. 'Today is the fifteenth of Ramadan, 1993,' she announced, 'and this house is so noisy I can barely hear myself think.' In the background, children were shouting, a television was blaring, and someone was asking loudly where his football had gone. Their father went completely still, because the boy searching for the football was him.

The recording went on for almost half an hour. There were short stories, a poem their father had recited for school, and a moment when young Saad accidentally knocked over a glass and everyone burst out laughing. Near the end, their grandmother's voice became gentler. 'One day these children will grow up and leave, and the house will be quiet,' she said. 'Abu Khalid, when that day comes, don't sit in silence. Make the tea, call the family, and let the noise come back.'

Nobody spoke for a long time after the tape clicked off. Uncle Saad was wiping his eyes, and Layan's father was staring out of the window, pretending to look at the street. 'We have to play it for Grandpa,' Layan said at last. Her father hesitated, worried that it might break his heart all over again. 'Or it might mend it,' Uncle Saad replied quietly, and after a while, her father nodded.

The next night, the whole family gathered in the majlis for the last time, surrounded by boxes and empty shelves. Uncle Saad had borrowed a portable cassette player from a friend, and Layan placed it on the small table in front of her grandfather. When her grandmother's voice began, his hands tightened on the arms of his chair, and for several agonising minutes his face showed nothing at all. Layan was beginning to regret the whole idea. Then came the crash of the broken glass, and suddenly her grandfather laughed, a real, deep laugh that none of them had heard in months.

'That glass,' he said, shaking his head, 'was from your grandmother's wedding set, and Saad told everyone the cat had done it.' Uncle Saad protested that he had been only seven, and the room erupted. For the next hour, their grandfather told story after story, each one reminding him of another, as though a door that had been locked for months had swung wide open. When the tape finished, he stood up slowly, went into the kitchen, and came back with a tray of tea. 'She always told me a house isn't made of walls,' he said. 'It's made of voices.'

Before they left, Layan noticed that the second side of the cassette was completely blank. So, with the old player on the table, the whole family recorded their own message: Omar's terrible jokes, her father's poem recited thirty years later, and their grandfather's slow, warm voice saying a prayer for the family. Layan then wrote a brand-new label in her neatest handwriting and stuck it beside her grandmother's. It said exactly the same thing: 'Open when the house is quiet.' As they drove to their new home, her grandfather held the tin on his lap, and for once, nobody felt like the house was quiet at all.

stories.title: The Man Who Caught the Light

pages.text: In the year 1011, Cairo was a city full of rumours, and fourteen-year-old Yusuf heard them all from his uncle's bookshop near the great mosque. The most exciting one was about a scholar from Basra called Ibn al-Haytham. People said he had boldly promised the Caliph that he could control the flooding of the mighty Nile. Some customers praised his courage, while others shook their heads. "That man has bitten off more than he can chew," muttered an old merchant, tapping his cup. "Nobody tells the river what to do."

A few months later, the scholar returned from his long journey south to Aswan, and Yusuf watched him ride past the shop. His shoulders were bent, and his face looked as grey as the dust on his robes. Word soon spread that he had studied the river carefully and realised the task was impossible with the tools of his time. Admitting this was a dangerous thing to do. The Caliph al-Hakim was not known for his patience, and men who disappointed him rarely kept their positions, or sometimes their lives.

Then a shocking piece of news reached the bookshop: Ibn al-Haytham had lost his mind. He had been shut away in a small house, and Yusuf's uncle, who had once sold him books, was asked to send him food every day. Nervously, Yusuf carried the first basket of bread and dates through the narrow streets. He expected to find a wild man shouting at the walls, but instead a calm figure looked up from a pile of papers. "Don't be afraid," the scholar whispered with a tired smile. "When every other door is locked, sometimes madness is the only one left open."

Yusuf kept the secret, and over the following weeks, he became the scholar's eyes and hands in the outside world. One afternoon, Ibn al-Haytham asked him to cover every window with thick cloth until the room was completely dark. Then he made a tiny hole, no bigger than a grain of rice, in the wooden shutter. Yusuf gasped as a picture slowly appeared on the opposite wall. It was the street outside, with its palm trees and passing donkeys, but everything was upside down!

"How is this possible?" Yusuf asked, reaching out to touch the moving colours. "Many great thinkers believed that our eyes send out rays to touch the things we see," the scholar explained. "But if that were true, we would be able to see in the dark, wouldn't we?" Yusuf thought for a moment and nodded slowly. "So the light must travel the other way," the scholar continued. "It comes from objects and enters the eye, just as it enters this room."

From then on, the dark room became a laboratory. Yusuf placed several candles outside the hole, and each one produced its own small spot of light on the wall. Whenever he covered a candle, its spot disappeared immediately, proving that light moved in straight lines. Ibn al-Haytham repeated every test again and again, writing down each result in careful detail. "Never accept an idea just because a famous name is attached to it," he told Yusuf. "Doubt is a scholar's best friend, and testing is the way we find the truth."

One morning, heavy footsteps sounded outside, and a guard's voice demanded to see the prisoner. Yusuf's heart was pounding as he pushed the papers under a rug just seconds before the door swung open. At once, Ibn al-Haytham began talking to a clay jug, asking it seriously about the price of onions. The guard rolled his eyes, glanced at the dark, messy room and left, clearly convinced the poor man was hopeless. When the footsteps had faded, the two of them sat in silence, and then they both tried very hard not to laugh.

For ten long years, the scholar continued his secret work, until the Caliph mysteriously disappeared in 1021. Only then did Ibn al-Haytham announce that he had recovered, and he walked out into the sunshine a free man. He went on to complete his famous Book of Optics, which explained how light and vision really work. Before leaving Cairo to continue his studies, he handed Yusuf a small wooden box with a tiny hole in one side. "You were my assistant when I had no one," he said warmly. "This discovery belongs to you as well."

Many years later, an elderly Yusuf would sit with his grandchildren and show them the upside-down world inside that little wooden box. Long after both men had passed away, the Book of Optics was translated into Latin and studied by scientists across Europe. His method of testing ideas carefully helped shape modern science itself. Today, every camera, from the largest telescope to the phone in your pocket, still uses the simple idea that was born in a dark room in Cairo. A hero, Yusuf always told the children, does not need a sword, only patience, honesty and the courage to ask questions.

pages.text: Faisal had built his weather station from a kit that his grandfather had given him two years earlier. It sat on the flat roof of their house in Taif, a white box full of sensors that sent readings to an old tablet in his bedroom. His sisters teased him about it and called him "the weatherman", and his cousin Turki said it was the most boring hobby he had ever heard of. Faisal didn't mind. He liked the idea that the sky was always telling a story, if only you knew how to read it.

That Thursday, the whole family was preparing for a weekend trip to a wadi an hour's drive away. Uncle Saad had found the perfect spot: a wide, sandy valley floor with acacia trees, far from the noise of the city. "Not a single cloud," he announced, holding up his phone. "The forecast says sunshine all weekend." Faisal glanced at his tablet and frowned. The air pressure had been falling steadily since the morning, faster than he had ever seen it fall before.

By the time they arrived, the sky above them was a perfect, cloudless blue. The men set up the tent while Faisal's mother and aunt unpacked the dates and Arabic coffee, and the younger children raced off to collect stones. Faisal, however, kept looking towards the mountains in the west. A line of dark grey cloud had appeared above the peaks, so far away that it looked almost harmless. "Relax," Turki said, throwing him a ball. "You're making a storm in a teacup."

Faisal tried to enjoy himself, but he couldn't shake off the feeling that something was wrong. He remembered a lesson from his geography teacher: rain that falls on distant mountains can rush down dry valleys miles away, even when the sky above them is clear. The ground in the wadi was hard and dry, so it would not absorb water quickly. He checked the old mud lines on the rocks around them, and they were higher than his head. Without realising it, his family had chosen to camp in the exact place where floods had passed before.

He found Uncle Saad by the fire. "Uncle, I think we should move the camp up to that ridge," he said, pointing to a rocky slope above the valley. His uncle laughed kindly. "Faisal, we've only just put the tent up, and if it rains, it will rain over there, not here." Faisal took a deep breath. "If water comes down this valley, we won't have time to pack anything, so please, just look at the clouds." His grandfather, who had been listening quietly, put down his coffee cup and looked.

The old man studied the mountains for a long moment. "When I was a boy, we called that kind of cloud a warning," he said. "My father never let us sleep on the valley floor after a sight like that." Nobody in the family ever argued with Grandfather, so, grumbling, they packed up the tent, loaded the cars and drove up the narrow track to the ridge. Turki complained the whole way that his cousin had ruined the weekend.

They had been on the ridge for less than an hour when they heard it: a low roar, like a distant aeroplane, growing louder by the second. Then a wall of brown water burst around the bend in the valley, carrying branches, rocks and even a broken fence. It swept across the sandy floor where their tent had stood not long before. The younger children screamed and clung to their mothers. Uncle Saad stood completely still, his face pale.

The flood lasted only twenty minutes, but when it had passed, the wadi looked like a different place. The acacia tree they had parked beside was half buried in mud, and their stone fire circle had disappeared completely. Uncle Saad put a hand on Faisal's shoulder. "I owe you an apology," he said quietly, "and probably a lot more than that." Turki didn't say anything at first, but later he sat down next to Faisal and asked him to explain how a barometer worked.

That night, under a sky full of stars, the family drank coffee on the ridge and told the story again and again. Grandfather said that Faisal had inherited his great-grandfather's eye for the weather. When they returned home, Faisal found a message on his tablet from Turki: "Can you help me build one of these?" He smiled and typed his reply. The sky had told its story, he thought, and this time someone had listened.

pages.text: Rakan had been staring at a blank canvas for three weeks, and the canvas had won every time. The regional art competition was only a month away, and his teacher, Mr Hamdan, had told the class, "Paint something that matters to you." It had sounded simple until Rakan actually tried. Everything he sketched looked either copied from the internet or painfully dull. One Friday afternoon, fed up, he grabbed his camera and wandered into the old streets of Al-Balad, hoping inspiration would find him.

The historic district of Jeddah was quiet in the heat, its tall coral-stone houses leaning together as if they were sharing secrets. Halfway down a narrow alley, Rakan stopped in front of a wooden door that had once been painted deep green. Its surface was covered in faded geometric patterns, stars inside stars and lines weaving over and under each other, most of them peeling and almost invisible. He took a photo without really knowing why. Then he went home and forgot all about it.

A week later, he returned, and something made him freeze. The top corner of the door had been carefully repainted, every star sharp and bright, the gold lines glowing against fresh green. Nobody on the street seemed to have noticed. Rakan compared it with his photo, his heart beating faster, because the repair was so precise that it must have taken hours. "Someone's bringing this door back to life," he whispered, "but who, and why in secret?"

Over the following weeks, the mystery deepened. Every Friday, another section of the pattern had reappeared, yet Rakan never caught a glimpse of the painter. He asked the man who ran the spice shop at the end of the alley, but he simply shrugged and said the house had been empty for years. Rakan was determined to get to the bottom of it. If the artist didn't work in the afternoon or the evening, he reasoned, there was only one time left.

So the next Friday he set his alarm, prayed Fajr with his father at the mosque, and hurried to Al-Balad as the sky turned pale blue. Sure enough, an elderly man was sitting on a folding stool in front of the door, a tiny brush in his hand. His hand trembled badly, and he had to wait, breathe and steady it before every single stroke. Rakan hesitated, then cleared his throat. "Assalamu alaikum, uncle," he said. "Are you the one who's been painting this?"

The old man, who introduced himself as Abu Saleh, smiled without taking his eyes off the brush. He explained that he had built and decorated this door with his own hands fifty years earlier, when he was a young craftsman. "My grandson has inherited the house, and he's planning to replace the door with a modern one," he said quietly. "I can't stop him, but I refuse to let it leave this world looking forgotten." He worked at dawn, he added, because the light was soft and his hands were steadier before the heat arrived.

Rakan came back every Friday after that, and Abu Saleh slowly turned him into an apprentice. On the first morning, instead of a brush, the old man handed him a battered metal compass. "Every pattern on this door begins with a single circle," he told him. "Rush the circle, and the whole design falls apart." Rakan, who had always wanted quick results, discovered that patience could be a skill in its own right. Line by line, the door glowed brighter, and his collection of photos grew.

When the competition deadline arrived, Rakan finally knew what mattered to him. He submitted a series of twelve photographs showing the door's journey from faded wood to living colour, alongside a painting of Abu Saleh's trembling hand holding the brush. He called it "One Circle at a Time". He didn't win first prize; he came second, but that turned out to be the least important part. One visitor at the exhibition, who happened to be Abu Saleh's grandson, stood in front of the photos for a long time without saying a word.

The following week, the green door was still there, and a small brass sign had been fixed beside it, explaining who had made it and when. The grandson had changed his mind, and he had decided to restore the house around the door instead of replacing it. Abu Saleh pressed the old compass into Rakan's hand. "It has drawn enough circles for me," he said. "Now it's your turn." Rakan went home, sat down in front of his canvas, and for the first time in weeks, he knew exactly where to begin.

pages.text: Hamad had been certain that a summer at his grandfather's house in Umluj would be the most boring month of his life. On the third morning, however, his sister Reem woke him before sunrise and pulled him down to the empty beach. In the cool, damp sand, they found two long, deep tracks leading from the waves up into the dunes. "They look like a small tractor came out of the sea," Hamad said, rubbing his eyes. Their grandfather, who had followed them with his coffee, smiled. "That was no tractor," he said. "A green turtle came here to lay her eggs."

A few metres away, someone had put a small fence of wooden sticks around a patch of sand. "The rangers from the marine reserve marked the nest weeks ago," Grandfather explained. "The eggs take about two months to hatch, so the babies could appear any night now." Reem, who wanted to study marine biology, immediately started writing in her notebook. Grandfather told them that the tiny turtles find the sea by following the moonlight shining on the water. "It's a long journey for something smaller than your hand," he added.

That evening, as they walked home, Hamad noticed something he had ignored before. On the hill above the beach, a new café had opened, and its bright white lights were pointing straight down at the sand. A large sign glowed above the door: Moonlight Café. Reem searched online and her face fell. "Listen to this," she said. "Artificial light confuses hatchlings, so they crawl towards the land instead of the sea, and most of them never survive."

The next afternoon, they visited the café to speak to the owner, a young man called Abu Saleh. He listened politely, but he shook his head when Reem asked him to switch off the lights at night. "I've put all my savings into this place," he said. "If customers can't see the café from the road, they won't stop, and I'll have to close." He laughed gently. "Besides, turtles have managed perfectly well for millions of years without my help."

Three nights later, Hamad couldn't sleep, so he walked down to check the nest. To his amazement, the sand inside the fence was moving, as if it were boiling. One by one, tiny dark heads were pushing up into the air. But instead of turning towards the sea, the hatchlings were crawling uphill, towards the bright lights and the busy road. Hamad called Reem, told her to wake Grandfather, and ran up the hill as fast as his legs would carry him.

He burst into the café, completely out of breath, and every customer turned to stare at him. "The turtles are hatching, and they're heading for the road!" he managed to say. For a moment, Abu Saleh just looked at him, clearly unsure what to do. Then he stepped outside and looked over the wall. Small shapes were already moving across the edge of the car park. Without another word, he hurried inside and switched off every light in the building.

Suddenly, the beach was dark, and the moon appeared, laying a silver path across the sea. Grandfather arrived with Reem, who was on the phone to a ranger. "She says we mustn't pick them up," Reem reported. "We should just keep the road blocked and let them find their own way." So the customers, Abu Saleh, and the family stood quietly in a long line between the hatchlings and the road. Slowly, as if they had suddenly remembered something, the little turtles turned around and began crawling towards the shining water.

It took almost an hour for the last hatchling to disappear into the waves. When the ranger arrived and counted the empty eggshells, she said that more than eighty babies had reached the sea. "If the lights had stayed on, we'd have lost most of them," she told Abu Saleh. He was silent for a long time, staring at the dark water. "I nearly made a terrible mistake," he finally admitted. "Thank goodness someone was paying attention."

A week later, the family returned to Moonlight Café and hardly recognised it. Abu Saleh had replaced the harsh white lights with soft orange ones that pointed down at the tables, not the beach. A new sign by the door read: A Turtle-Friendly Café. Surprisingly, business was better than ever, because people came hoping to see a nest. As Hamad sipped his mango juice, he realised that this had turned out to be the best summer of his life, and he was already counting the days until the next one.

options: He was angry with Hamad for causing problems

stories.title: The Secret on the Seventh Floor

pages.text: Huda had lived on the seventh floor of the same building in Jeddah for as long as she could remember. From her bedroom window, she could see the sea shining between the towers, and if she leaned out a little, she could see her neighbour's balcony. It belonged to Umm Saad, an elderly widow who had always seemed to Huda like a quiet queen among her plants. Jasmine, mint and tiny lemon trees had filled that balcony for years, and in the evenings their smell drifted across to Huda's room like a gentle greeting.

That spring, however, everything in Huda's own home changed. Her father's company had closed without warning, and although he tried to stay cheerful, Huda often heard her parents talking in low, worried voices late at night. Then, out of the blue, something strange began to happen. Every Thursday morning, a cloth bag was left outside their door, containing fresh bread, dates and sometimes a box of sweets. There was never a note, and nobody in the family could guess who had left it.

At around the same time, Huda noticed that Umm Saad's balcony was slowly dying. The jasmine had turned brown, the mint leaves were drooping, and the little lemon trees looked thirsty and tired. Her mother explained that Umm Saad's only son had recently moved abroad for work, and that the old lady now found it hard to carry heavy watering cans. "She's too proud to ask anyone for help," her mother sighed. That night, Huda lay awake, staring at the dry plants, and an idea slowly began to grow in her mind.

The next morning, Huda woke before dawn, while the city was still blue and silent. She had found an old garden hose in the storage cupboard and fixed it to the tap on her own balcony. Holding her breath, she stretched her arm as far as it would go and sent a thin stream of water over the low wall onto Umm Saad's plants. Suddenly, a light switched on inside her neighbour's flat, and Huda ducked down so quickly that she nearly dropped the hose. Her heart was pounding, but after a minute the light went off again, and she realised she had not been caught.

For the next few weeks, Huda kept up her secret routine, getting up early every morning before school. Little by little, the balcony came back to life: green leaves appeared, and the first white jasmine flowers opened like small stars. Huda noticed that Umm Saad had started sitting outside again in the evenings, smiling as she touched the new leaves. Meanwhile, the mysterious bag still arrived every Thursday without fail. "Whoever is doing this," her father said one morning, his voice thick with emotion, "they have a heart of gold."

Then, one evening in late April, a powerful dust storm swept across the city. The sky turned an angry orange, the wind howled between the buildings, and Huda's family hurried to close every window. Through the glass, Huda saw several of Umm Saad's pots crash onto the balcony floor. What worried her more, however, was that her neighbour's flat was completely dark, even though it was barely eight o'clock. "Something's wrong," Huda said firmly. "Umm Saad never goes to bed this early."

Huda and her mother rushed across the corridor and knocked loudly on Umm Saad's door. At first there was no answer, but then they heard a weak voice calling from inside. Fortunately, Huda's mother remembered that Umm Saad had once given them a spare key in case of emergencies. They found the old lady on the kitchen floor; she had slipped while trying to reach a torch when the electricity went off. While her mother called an ambulance, Huda held Umm Saad's hand and kept talking to her calmly so that she would not feel afraid.

As they waited, Umm Saad looked at Huda with a tired but amused smile. "I know it's you who has been watering my plants," she whispered. "I saw your little hose one morning, but I didn't want to spoil your secret." Huda's cheeks went red, but before she could reply, the old lady added something that left her speechless. "And I suppose I should confess, too," she said. "Those Thursday bags didn't appear by magic, my dear."

Thankfully, Umm Saad had only sprained her wrist, and she was back home within two days. Soon afterwards, Huda's father found a new job, and the first thing the family did was invite their neighbour for dinner. Now Huda no longer waters the balcony in secret; instead, she visits every Thursday afternoon, and the two of them look after the plants together while sharing tea and stories. Sometimes Huda thinks about how two quiet acts of kindness had been passing each other in the dark, each one unseen. She has learned that the kindest people rarely ask for thanks, but they always, somehow, find each other.

stories.title: The Song of the White Stone

pages.text: Faisal had always thought his grandfather's songs were just old-fashioned noise. Every evening on the Farasan Islands, Grandfather would sit on the porch and hum the same long chant he had learned as a young pearl diver, decades before Faisal was born. "It's longer than a football match," Faisal whispered to his sister, Lama, who rolled her eyes but secretly knew every word. Neither of them imagined that, within a week, those strange lines would mean the difference between getting home and being lost at sea.

The trip was Uncle Saad's idea. He had borrowed a friend's small fishing boat and promised to show them the dolphins that played near the outer reefs. The morning was perfect, and the water was so clear that they could see shoals of silver fish darting beneath the hull. Lama took dozens of photos, while Faisal trailed his hand in the warm sea and wondered why anyone would ever want to live in a city.

Trouble started in the afternoon. The engine coughed twice, made a horrible grinding sound, and then fell silent. Uncle Saad tried everything he could think of, but as he leaned over the back of the boat, a wave rocked them and he slipped, landing hard on his wrist. "It's only a sprain," he insisted through gritted teeth, though his face had turned pale. When Lama checked the radio, she discovered that its battery was completely flat, and none of their phones had a signal.

For a while, nobody spoke. The current was carrying them steadily away from the islands they knew, and the sun was sinking towards the horizon. "Right," said Uncle Saad, trying to keep a cool head. "We have water, we have oars, and we have each other. We're all in the same boat, literally." Faisal laughed despite himself, but he could not stop staring at the empty, darkening sea.

It was Lama who first noticed the bright star rising low in the south. "Faisal," she said slowly, "what's the line in Grandfather's song about Suhail?" He frowned, and then the words came back to him as clearly as if Grandfather were sitting beside them: "When Suhail climbs above your left shoulder, row until the white stone stands before you." Uncle Saad stared at them in amazement. "The old divers used songs like that to find their way home," he said. "Your grandfather has been teaching you a map all these years, and you didn't even realise it."

Since Uncle Saad couldn't use his injured wrist, the two teenagers took the oars. They turned the boat until Suhail shone above Faisal's left shoulder and began to row, slowly at first and then in a steady rhythm. Their arms burned and their palms soon became sore, but they kept going, singing the chant under their breath to keep time. Hours seemed to pass before Lama suddenly stopped and pointed. Ahead of them, pale in the moonlight, stood a tall rock shaped like a finger.

"The white stone," Faisal breathed. Behind it lay a small sandy bay, sheltered from the wind, where they could anchor safely. According to the next verse, a ruined watchtower should be visible on the hill above, and sure enough, a crumbling stone tower was outlined against the stars. Uncle Saad handed Lama his torch. "If anyone is searching for us, they'll be looking from the sea," he said. "Climb up there, flash it three times, wait a minute, and then do it again."

Lama scrambled up the slope while Faisal stayed with their uncle, whose wrist had swollen badly. For nearly an hour she sent her signal into the darkness, and just as her hope was beginning to fade, a powerful beam of light swept across the water in reply. Twenty minutes later, a coast guard boat entered the bay, and a smiling officer explained that Grandfather had raised the alarm as soon as they had failed to return before sunset. "He told us to check near the white stone," the officer added. "He said that if you remembered his song, that's exactly where you'd be."

When they finally reached home, Grandfather was waiting on the porch, just as he always was. He hugged each of them, examined Uncle Saad's bandaged wrist, and then turned to Faisal with a twinkle in his eye. "So," he said, "is my song still longer than a football match?" Faisal grinned sheepishly and admitted, "It's longer, Grandfather, but it's much more useful." That evening, when the old man began to hum, both teenagers sat beside him and asked him to teach them every single verse.

pages.text: Faisal had always thought that summer at his grandfather's house near Umluj was the most boring way to spend a holiday. There was no shopping mall, the internet was painfully slow, and his grandfather went to bed straight after the Isha prayer. His younger sister, Noura, on the other hand, loved every minute of it. "You'll change your mind this year," she told him as they unpacked their bags. "Grandfather says something amazing is about to happen on the beach."

Grandfather Saleh had been a fisherman for forty years, but now he volunteered with a team that protected green turtles along the Red Sea coast. The next morning, he led them to a small area of sand surrounded by wooden sticks. "A mother turtle laid over a hundred eggs here almost two months ago," he explained. "They could hatch any night now." He told them that baby turtles find the sea by crawling towards the brightest part of the horizon, which is usually the moonlight shining on the water. "Whatever happens, never touch them," he added firmly.

There was one problem, however. A new café had opened on the hill behind the beach, and every evening it was decorated with hundreds of bright white lights. Grandfather had already spoken to the owner, but the young man hadn't taken him seriously. To make matters worse, Grandfather had to drive their grandmother to a hospital appointment in Tabuk that afternoon, and they wouldn't be back until the following day. "If anything happens, call Abu Ahmed from the turtle team," he said, handing Faisal a piece of paper with a phone number on it.

That night, Faisal couldn't sleep, so he and Noura sat on the terrace overlooking the beach. Suddenly, Noura grabbed his arm and pointed at the sand. At first, it looked as if the beach itself was moving, but then Faisal realised that dozens of tiny turtles were pushing their way out of the nest. His heart sank as he watched them crawl not towards the sea, but up the beach towards the café and the busy road beside it. He called Abu Ahmed immediately, but he was at least forty minutes away.

Without thinking, Faisal reached for his phone to switch on the torch. "Stop!" Noura cried. "Grandfather said white light confuses them even more." Faisal felt foolish, but there was no time to waste on feeling embarrassed. They couldn't carry the turtles to the water, and they certainly couldn't wait for help to arrive. "Stay here and keep the crabs away from them," he said, and he ran up the hill towards the café.

The café was crowded with families enjoying the cool evening, and the owner, a young man called Khalid, was busy serving tea. Breathlessly, Faisal explained what was happening and begged him to turn off the lights. "Turn off the lights on a Thursday night because of some turtles?" Khalid laughed. "If you don't, by morning they'll all be dead on that road," Faisal replied, surprised at how steady his voice sounded. An elderly man at a nearby table put down his cup and said quietly, "The boy is right, my son." For a long moment Khalid hesitated, and then he reached for the switch.

The hill fell into darkness, and slowly the silver path of the moon on the sea became the brightest thing in sight. Faisal hurried back down to the beach, hardly daring to breathe. One by one, the little turtles stopped, turned around and began to make their way towards the waves. Noura was kneeling on the sand, gently waving away a ghost crab that had come too close. Behind them, the café customers had gathered at the edge of the beach with their phones in their pockets, watching in complete silence.

Just as most of the hatchlings reached the water, headlights appeared and Abu Ahmed jumped out of his car. He switched on a small red torch and found one last turtle trapped upside down in a tyre track. Wearing gloves, he carefully turned it over and watched it race towards the sea. "Ninety-four made it," he announced after checking the tracks. "Only about one in a thousand baby turtles survives to become an adult, so tonight every single one counts."

When Grandfather returned the next day, he listened to the whole story without saying a word, but his eyes were shining with pride. That afternoon, Khalid knocked on the door to tell them he had replaced the white lights with soft orange ones that faced away from the beach. "I've even put up a sign saying 'Turtle-Friendly Café'," he said with an embarrassed smile. Faisal asked his grandfather whether he could help record the next nest, which was due to hatch in two weeks. For the first time in his life, he found himself wishing that the summer would last a little longer.

pages.text: Faris had been staying at his grandmother's house in old Jeddah for only three days when he noticed the light. It appeared in the tall coral-stone house across the narrow lane, a building that had been locked up for months while it was being restored. Every evening, workers in dusty overalls left at sunset, and the heavy wooden door was bolted behind them. So who could possibly be switching on a light on the roof at nine o'clock at night? Faris leaned closer to the carved wooden window and frowned.

"It's probably just a reflection from a car," said his sister Lama, without looking up from her book. "Cars don't drive on the roof," Faris replied, pointing. The light flashed again: short, short, short, then long, long, long. Lama finally put her book down and joined him at the window. For a moment, neither of them said a word.

The next morning, over sweet tea and dates, they told their grandmother what they had seen. She smiled and explained that the house had once belonged to a wealthy pearl merchant, nearly a century ago. "The neighbourhood children say it's haunted," she added, rolling her eyes, "but people have been telling silly stories about that house since I was a girl." Faris wasn't convinced by ghosts, but he wasn't convinced by reflections either. Something strange was going on, and he was determined to get to the bottom of it.

That evening, Faris set an alarm for a quarter to nine and waited by the window with his phone ready. At exactly nine o'clock, the light began again, and this time he recorded the whole thing. The flashes went on for almost five minutes before they stopped suddenly. "It must be a pattern," he whispered. "Nobody turns a torch on and off like that by accident."

Lama watched the video three times, her eyes growing wider each time. "I know what this is," she said slowly. "We learned Morse code in my robotics club last year. Three short, three long, three short means SOS. It's a call for help!" She grabbed a pencil and began writing down the letters as Faris played the video at half speed.

Letter by letter, a message appeared on the paper: S-O-S... R-O-O-F... D-O-O-R... L-O-C-K-E-D... H-U-R-T. The two of them stared at each other in shock. If Lama was right, someone had been trapped on that roof, perhaps for more than a day. "We have to tell Teta now," Faris said, already running towards the stairs.

Their grandmother didn't waste a second once she had seen the message. She phoned the man in charge of the restoration, whose number was printed on a sign outside, and then she called Civil Defence. Within twenty minutes, the quiet lane was full of flashing lights and curious neighbours in their nightclothes. Rescuers unlocked the great wooden door and climbed the steep staircase, and Faris held his breath as he watched from below.

A few minutes later, they carried down an elderly man with a bandaged ankle and a small torch in his hand. His name was Uncle Saleh, and he was the night watchman who checked the building after the workers had gone home. He explained that the wind had slammed the roof door shut behind him, and he had twisted his ankle trying to force it open. His phone battery had died, so he had relied on something he had learned forty years earlier as a radio operator on a cargo ship. "I kept signalling," he said with a tired smile, "and I prayed that somebody would understand."

A week later, Uncle Saleh knocked at their door, leaning on a walking stick and holding a small wooden box. Inside was an old brass Morse key, polished until it shone. "This travelled across every ocean with me," he told Lama, "and now it belongs to someone who still knows how to listen." He turned to Faris and shook his hand warmly. "And thank you for noticing what everyone else ignored," he said. From then on, the old house across the lane never looked haunted again to Faris; it looked like a place where a mystery had been solved.

pages.text: For as long as Omar could remember, Khalid's bedroom window had been exactly opposite his own, across a narrow street in Al-Khobar. When they were nine, the two boys had invented a secret code using torches: one flash meant "yes", two meant "no", and three short flashes followed by a long one meant "Are you there?" Every night before sleep, they would send messages across the dark gap between the buildings. Their parents laughed and called it the world's slowest internet. But for Omar, that small circle of light had always meant one thing: he was never alone.

By the time they turned fourteen, however, things had begun to change. Khalid had been chosen for a football academy, and he now spent most evenings training with a group of older boys Omar barely knew. Omar, on the other hand, preferred his science projects, and the two friends were slowly drifting apart. Still, they had promised to build one thing together: a small solar-powered water purifier for the school science fair. They had worked on it for weeks, and Khalid had sworn he would be there to help present it.

On the morning of the fair, Omar stood beside their project, checking the door again and again. Khalid never came. Omar had to explain everything to the judges alone, his voice shaking, and although they won third place, the prize felt empty. That evening, he saw three short flashes and one long one from across the street. For the first time in five years, he closed his curtains without answering.

For the next two weeks, Omar ignored the light. At school, he walked past Khalid in the corridor as if he had become invisible, and whenever Khalid tried to speak, Omar found an excuse to leave. "He's chosen his new friends," he told his grandfather, who lived with the family. "That's fine. I don't need him." His grandfather looked at him over his glasses and said quietly, "A friendship of years shouldn't be thrown away because of one bad day, my son." Omar pretended not to hear.

Then came the night of the sandstorm. Omar's parents had driven to Dammam to visit his aunt, who was ill, and he had been left to keep an eye on his grandfather. Just after ten o'clock, the wind grew so strong that the windows rattled, and suddenly every light in the building went out. In the darkness, Omar heard his grandfather coughing, then struggling to breathe. With trembling hands, Omar found his phone, only to realise that the battery was completely dead.

He searched the apartment desperately, but the landline had been disconnected years ago and the neighbours on their floor were away. Through the window, the street had disappeared behind a wall of brown dust. Then Omar remembered the old torch in his desk drawer. Pressing it against the glass, he flashed the emergency signal they had agreed on as children but never once used: long, long, long, which meant "Come now." He had no idea whether anyone would see it through the storm.

For a terrible minute, there was nothing. Then a tiny light appeared across the street and flashed once: yes. Within ten minutes, there was loud knocking at the door, and Khalid rushed in with his father, both of them covered in dust. Khalid's father, who was a nurse, helped Omar's grandfather sit up and gave him his inhaler, which had fallen behind the sofa in the dark. Then they carried him carefully down the stairs to the car and drove slowly through the storm to the hospital.

By midnight, the doctor had confirmed that Omar's grandfather would be fine, though he would need to stay for the night. Sitting in the quiet waiting room, Omar finally broke the silence. "Why didn't you come to the fair?" he asked. Khalid stared at his hands for a long moment before replying. "My dad had arranged a trial with a professional club that morning without asking me, and I didn't have the courage to tell him I'd made a promise to you," he admitted. "I should have called you, but I was too ashamed, and then you stopped answering."

Omar realised that he had been so busy feeling hurt that he had never once asked what had happened. "I'm sorry too," he said. "I should have answered your signal." A month later, when their purifier was sent to the regional competition, Khalid stood beside him in front of the judges, explaining every part as proudly as if he had built it alone. That night, back in their rooms, three short flashes and a long one shone across the street. Omar smiled, picked up his torch, and answered: yes, still here.
